Also among some migration communities along [[Huatung Valley]]. | ethnicity = [[Taivoan people|Taivoan]] | extinct = end of 19th century | familycolor = Austronesian | fam2 = [[East Formosan languages|East Formosan]] | fam3 = [[Sirayaic languages|Sirayaic]] | fam4 = Taivoan–Makatao | script = [[Latin script|Latin]] ([[Sinckan Manuscripts]]), [[Han characters]] ([[Traditional Chinese|traditional]]) | iso3 = tvx | isoexception = dialect | map = Formosan languages 2008.png | mapcaption = (pink) Taivoan | coordinates = {{coord|23|06|N|120|27|E|type:landmark|display=inline}} | glotto = taiv1237 | glottorefname = Taivoan | lingua = 30-FAA-bb | revived = revitalization movement }} '''Taivoan''' or '''Taivuan''', is a [[Formosan languages|Formosan language]] spoken until the end of the 19th century by the indigenous [[Taivoan people]] of [[Taiwan]]. Taivoan used to be regarded as a dialect of [[Siraya language|Siraya]], but now more evidence has shown that they should be classified as separate languages. The corpora previously regarded as Siraya like the [[Gospel of Matthew|Gospel of St. Matthew]] and the Notes on Formulary of Christianity translated into "Siraya" by the Dutch people in the 17th century should be in Taivoan majorly. Since the January 2019 code release, [[SIL International]] has recognized Taivoan as an independent language and assigned the code '''tvx'''.{{Cite web|url=https://iso639-3.sil.org/code/tvx|title=639 Identifier Documentation: tvx|date=2019-01-25|website=SIL International|access-date=2019-01-29}} == Classification == The Taivoan language used to be regarded as a dialect of Siraya. However, more evidences have shown that it belongs to an independent language spoken by the [[Taivoan people]]. === Documentary evidence === In ''De Dagregisters van het Kasteel Zeelandia'' written by the Dutch colonizers during 1629–1662, it was clearly said that when the Dutch people would like to speak to the chieftain of Cannacannavo ([[Kanakanavu people|Kanakanavu]]), they needed to translate from [[Dutch language|Dutch]] to Sinckan (Siraya), from Sinckan to [[Tarroequan]] (possibly a [[Paiwan language|Paiwan]] or a [[Rukai language|Rukai]] language), from Tarroequan to Taivoan, and from Taivoan to [[Kanakanavu language|Cannacannavo]].{{Cite book |url=http://resources.huygens.knaw.nl/retroboeken/taiwan/ |title=De Dagregisters van het Kasteel Zeelandia, Taiwan: 1629–1662 |date=1986 |publisher=M. Nijhoff |location=ʼS-Gravenhage |language=nl}}{{Cite book |last=Lee |first=Jui-Yuan |title=From Single to Group: The Formation of Sideia in the 17th Century |publisher=Department of History: National Cheng Kung University |year=2015}}
"...... in Cannacannavo: Aloelavaos tot welcken de vertolckinge in Sinccans, Tarrocquans en Tevorangs geschiede, weder voor een jaer aengenomen" — ''De Dagregisters van het Kasteel Zeelandia'', pp.6–8
According to [[William Campbell (missionary)|William Campbell]]'s ''[[Formosa Under the Dutch]]'' (1903), historical records show that various displaced indigenous groups "spoke several languages in the same place." Despite this linguistic diversity, populations including the Taivoan ("Tevorangians") were forced to mechanically memorize the Sinckan catechism by heart:{{Cite book |last=William |first=Campbell |title=Formosa under the Dutch: described from contemporary records, with explanatory notes and a bibliography of the island |publisher=Kegan Paul |year=1903 |location=London |pages=241 |language=English |chapter=From the Tayouan Consistory}}
"It also often occurred that people living among the mountains were enticed by all possible means to come down and live in the valleys or plains. The people thus got mixed, and spoke several languages in the same place; one result being that, in keeping with the usual routine, those persons learnt the catechism of Mr. Junius by heart; but, while doing so, they acted just like magpies in repeating what has been said to them. And yet, people of this type received  baptism; for Mr. Gravius informed us that he had met several Tevorangians who had been baptized under those unusual conditions. "— ''Formosa Under the Dutch'', p.241

''Tree based on the relative chronology of sound changes'' * '''Sirayaic''' ** ''Siraya'' ** Taivoan–Makatao *** ''Taivoan'' *** ''Makatao'' Li (2009) considers the second tree (the one containing the Taivoan–Makatao group) to be the somewhat more likely one. === Criticism against Candidius' famous assertion === Taivoan was considered by some scholars as a dialectal subgroup of the Siraya ever since [[George Candidius]] included "Tefurang" in the eight Siraya villages which he claimed all had "the same manners, customs and religion, and speak the same language."{{Cite book |last=Campbell |first=William |url=https://archive.org/details/formosaunderdut00campgoog |title=Formosa under the Dutch: Described from Contemporary Records |publisher=Kegan Paul |year=1903 |location=London |pages=[https://archive.org/details/formosaunderdut00campgoog/page/n31 9] |isbn=978-957-638-083-9 |language=en}} However, American linguist [[Raleigh Ferrell]] reexaminates the Dutch materials and says "it appear that the Tevorangians were a distinct ethnolinguistic group, differing markedly in both language and culture from the Siraya." Ferrell mentions that, given that Candidius asserted that he was well familiar with the eight supposed Siraya villages including Tevorang, it's extremely doubtful that he ever actually visited the latter: "it is almost certain, in any case, that he had not visited Tevorang when he wrote his famous account in 1628. The first Dutch visit to Tevorang appears to have been in January 1636 [...]"{{Cite journal |last=Ferrell |first=Raleigh |date=1971 |title=Aboriginal Peoples of the Southwestern Taiwan Plains |journal=Bulletin of the Institute of Ethnology |language=en |volume=32 |pages=217–235}} Lee (2015) regards that, when Siraya was a [[lingua franca]] among at least eight indigenous communities in southwestern Taiwan plain, [[Taivoan people]] from Tevorangh, who has been proved to have their own language in "De Dagregisters van het Kasteel Zeelandia", might still need the translation service from Wanli, a neighbor community that shared common hunting field and also a militarily alliance with Tevorangh. Li noted in his "The Lingue Franche in Taiwan" that, [[Siraya language|Siraya]] exerted its influence over neighbouring languages in the southwestern plains in Taiwan, including Taivoan to the east and [[Makatao language|Makatao]] to the South in the 17th century, and became lingua franca in the whole area.{{Cite book |last=Li |first=Paul Jen-kuei |title=Atlas of Languages of Intercultural Communication in the Pacific, Asia, and the Americas |date=1996 |publisher=De Gruyter Mouton |editor-last=Wurm |editor-first=Stephen A. |location=Berlin |language=en |chapter=The Lingue Franche in Taiwan |editor-last2=Mühlhäusler |editor-first2=Peter |editor-last3=Tryon |editor-first3=Darrell T.}} == Phonology == The following is the phonology of the language:{{Cite book|title=Phonology and Spelling System Reconstruction|last=Alexander|first=Adelaar|publisher=Siraya languages study and revival seminars|year=2014}} === Vowels === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" ! ! The sound also clearly appears in a recording of the typical Taivoan ceremonial song "Kalawahe" sung by Taivoan in [[Lakku]] that belongs to Vogavon dialect.{{Cite web |date=2012-12-23 |title=Gāoxióng Xiàn Dàwǔlǒng qún qiān xì---Kalawahe (jiālāwǎhēi) liù guī xīnglóng pān ānrán lǐngchàng/wángshùhuā dá chàng |script-title=zh:高雄縣大武壟群牽戲---Kalawahe(加拉瓦嘿) 六龜興隆潘安然領唱/王樹花答唱 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tW5WzapZYLk |access-date=2018-05-30 |website=YouTube |language=zh}} The digraph ''ts'' recorded in the early 20th century may represent {{IPA|/t͡sʰ/}} or {{IPA|/t͡s/}}: * {{IPA|/t͡sʰ/}} or {{IPA|/t͡s/}}: ma'''ts'''a (door, gate), tabu'''ts'''uk (spear), '''ts'''aki'''ts'''ak (arrow), ma'''ts'''ihaha (to laugh), '''ts'''ukun (elbow), a'''ts'''ipi (a sole of the foot), '''ts'''au (dog). Only one word is attested in Vogavon dialect in Lakku: ka'''ts'''ui (pants, trousers). Some scholars in [[Formosan languages]] suggest it is not likely that {{IPA|/t͡sʰ/}} and {{IPA|/t͡s/}} appear in a Formosan language simultaneously, and therefore '''ts''' may well represent {{IPA|/t͡s/}} as '''c''' does, not {{IPA|/t͡sʰ/}}. === Stress === It is hard to tell the actual stressing system of Taivoan in the 17th–19th century, as it has been a dormant language for nearly a hundred years. However, since nearly all the existing Taivoan words but the numerals pronounced by the elders fall on the final syllable, there has been a tendency to stress on the final syllable in modern Taivoan for language revitalization and education, compared to modern [[Siraya language|Siraya]] that the penultimate syllable is stressed. == Grammar == === Pronouns === The Taivoan personal pronouns are listed below with all the words without asterisk being attested in corpora in the 20th century : {| class="wikitable" !Type of Pronoun !Independent !Nominative !Genitive !Oblique |- !1s |''iau'' |''kuri'' |''-ku'' |''iyaw-an'' |- !2s |''imhu'' |''ko'' |''-ho'' |''imhu-an'' |- !3s |''*teni'' |''*ta teni'' |''-tin'' |''*tini-an'' |- !1p.i |''*imita'' |''kita'' |''*-(m)ita'' |''*imita-n'' |- !1p.e |''*imian'' |''*kame'' |''*-(m)ian'' |''*imian-an'' |- !2p |''imomi'' |''kamo, kama'' |''*-(m)omi'' |''imomi-an'' |- !3p |''*naini'' |''*ta naini'' |''-nin'' |''*naini-an'' |} == Numerals == Taivoan has a decimal numeral system as following: {| class="wikitable" |+Taivoan Numerals |1 |tsaha{{hamza}} |11 |saka |- |2 |ruha |12 |bazun |- |3 |toho |13 |kuzun |- |4 |paha{{hamza}} |14 |langlang |- |5 |hima |15 |linta |- |6 |lom |16 |takuba |- |7 |kito{{hamza}} |17 |kasin |- |8 |kipa{{hamza}} |18 |kumsim |- |9 |matuha |19 |tabatak |- |10 |kaipien |20 |kaitian |- ! colspan="4" |Examples of higher numerals |- |30 | colspan="3" |tu-tuhu kaipien |- |60 | colspan="3" |lo-lom kaipien |- |99 | colspan="3" |matuha kaipien ab ki matuha |- |100 | colspan="3" |ka{{hamza}}atuxan |- |4,000 | colspan="3" |paha{{hamza}} katununan |- |5,000 | colspan="3" |hima katununan |} == Examples == === Words and phrases === [[File:六重溪部落大滿語祭歌歌詞.jpg|thumb|400x400px|Taivoan ritual song spelled in [[Chinese characters]] in [[Liuchongxi]], [[Tainan]].]] Some Taivoan people in remote communities like [[Siaolin Village|Siaolin]], [[Alikuan]], [[Laolong]], [[Fangliao (Kaohsiung)|Fangliao]], and [[Dazhuang, Hualien County, Taiwan|Dazhuang]], especially the elders, still use some Taivoan words nowadays, such as ''miunun'' "welcome" (originally "please be seated"), ''mahanru'' (in Siaolin, Alikuan), ''makahanru'' (in Laolong) "thank you", "goodbye" (originally "beautiful"), ''tapakua'' "wait a moment". === Songs === Many Taivoan songs have been recorded and some ceremonial songs like "Kalawahe" and "Taboro" are still sung during every Night Ceremony annually. Some examples are: ==== Kalawahe (or "the Song out of [[Kong-kài|the Shrine]]")==== Source:{{Citation |last=Taivoan Dance Theatre |date=2015 |location=Kaohsiung |publisher=Taivoan Dance Theatre |language=zh |script-title=zh:歡喜來牽戲 (Let's Dance a Round Dance)}} : Wa-he. Manie, he mahanru e, he kalawahe, wa-he. : Talaloma e, he talaloma e, he kalawahe, wa-he. : Tamaku e, he tamaku e, he kalawahe, wa-he. : Saviki e, he saviki e, he kalawahe, wa-he. : Rarom he, he rarom he, he kalawahe, wa-he. ==== Panga (or "the Song of Offerings") ==== : Ho i he, rarom mahanru ho i he, rarom taipanga ho i he. : Ho i he, hahu mahanru ho i he, hahu taipanga ho i he. : Ho i he, hana mahanru ho i he, hana taipanga ho i he. : Ho i he, saviki mahanru ho i he, saviki taipanga ho i he. : Ho i he, iruku mahanru ho i he, tuku taipanga ho i he. == See also == * [[Taivoan people]] * [[Sinckan Manuscripts]] ==Notes== {{Reflist|group=note|30em}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Incubator|code= tvx}} {{Languages of Taiwan}} {{Formosan languages}} [[Category:Formosan languages]] [[Category:Extinct languages of Asia]] [[Category:Languages extinct in the 19th century]] [[Category:Taivoan culture]]
